transcript.text: Samsung RS68A8820S9/EU flashing 22E on the display and the fridge side isn't as cold as it should be. What does 22E mean and can I fix it?

On Samsung models, code 22E typically indicates a fault with the fridge evaporator fan—either it isn't spinning because of an obstruction (usually ice buildup), or the motor itself has failed. This aligns with your symptom: if the fan that pushes cold air from the freezer into the fridge stops working, the fridge warms up while the freezer stays cold. To fix this, we first need to confirm whether it's a simple blockage caused by a defrost fault or a genuine motor failure. Please check:
1. Is the freezer compartment still freezing properly (solid ice cubes)?
2. When you open the freezer door and press the door switch (to turn off the light), do you hear the fan running inside? If it's hard to hear, put your ear near the vent at the top back of the fridge section. Let me know these two things so I can guide you through the next safe check.

The freezer seems fine and the ice maker is still making ice. I can't clearly hear a fan running, and the airflow from the fridge vents is very weak. There's an occasional ticking/scraping sound from the back panel inside the fridge. No burning smell and nothing tripping, if that matters.

The 22E code combined with weak airflow and no clear fan noise suggests the evaporator fan is either seized by ice or has failed. However, in Samsung frost-free fridge-freezers like yours, a 'dead' fan is often just an effect of something else: if the automatic defrost system fails (usually the heater element, the thermal fuse/thermostat, or the sensor), ice builds up over the evaporator coils at the back of the freezer. This ice chokes off the airflow to the fridge and can jam the fan blades. The 'ticking' sound you hear is likely metal contracting/expanding as it cools, or possibly ice shifting, which fits with an iced-up system. To tell if this is a simple blockage (which we can clear) or a part failure (which needs replacement), we need to see what's behind the panels. The only safe way to do that on a frost-free fridge is a full manual defrost. Please switch it off at the wall, empty the freezer, and leave the doors open until all ice has melted completely. Dry everything out thoroughly, then plug it back in and run it for a few hours. Let me know:
1. Did the fridge side get cold again after this?
2. When you looked inside the freezer during the defrost, was there a solid block of ice on the back wall (evaporator cover), or was it fairly clear? If the cooling returns but the problem comes back in a week or two, we will know for sure that one of the defrost components has failed and needs replacing. If it doesn't cool at all even after a full defrost, then the fan motor itself is likely dead.

I did the full defrost. The code cleared and the fridge got cold again, but 22E came back about 10 days later and it's the same problem again. I didn't really look at the back wall of the freezer, so I can't say if there was a solid block of ice. I can't take the inner back panel off, so I won't be doing that.

The fact that a full manual defrost temporarily fixed the cooling but the 22E code and warm fridge returned after about 10 days suggests this is not just ice blocking the fan—it is a fault in the automatic defrost system. In your Samsung model, one of three parts has likely failed: the defrost heater element (which melts the ice), the defrost thermal fuse/thermostat (which cuts power to the heater if it gets too hot or fails open), or the defrost sensor (which tells the board when to start a defrost cycle). Because you cannot remove the inner back panel of the freezer, we cannot visually confirm the ice blockage or access these components. These parts are located behind that panel and require specific tools and knowledge to test safely with a multimeter. This is an engineer-only repair. You will need a qualified appliance technician to:
1. Remove the rear freezer panel.
2. Test the continuity of the defrost heater, thermal fuse, and sensor.
3. Replace whichever component has failed (usually the heater or the fuse).
4. Clear any remaining ice blockage from the evaporator coils. Please contact a repair engineer. Do not attempt to remove panels while the appliance is plugged in.
